name: AI clipping for creators
what: Cut creators' long-form videos into short clips using AI editing tools, post them to TikTok and Reels, and get paid per view through marketplaces like Content Rewards.
pitch: Big creators have hours of unused footage sitting around, and short clips are the easiest way for them to reach new fans, so they'll pay you for posting clips that gain traction.
best: Someone looking for the lowest possible barrier to entry, more as a way to learn content and AI tools than as a long-term income plan.
truth: Tilbury is direct about this one: competition is very high, because it's this easy to start, everyone jumps in. Most people quit within a week or two, so simple consistency puts you ahead of most, but the ceiling on income is modest.

name: Pet waste (dog poop) removal service
cost: Very low startup cost (~$500 for basic equipment)
what: Offer a recurring weekly service that shows up at a customer's home, cleans up dog waste from the yard, sanitizes the turf, and leaves, using simple tools: a rake, scoop, waste bins, disinfectant, and gloves.
pitch: Zaback cites U.S. pet-ownership data (66% of households own a pet, 65 million own at least one dog producing over 20 billion pounds of waste a year) and a real example he watched personally: a scooper who built a 300-customer route, did about 30 jobs a day per employee, and grossed roughly $20,000 a month, over a quarter million a year, charging an average of $69 per customer per month.
best: Someone comfortable with genuinely unglamorous, hands-on outdoor work who's building toward a recurring-revenue route rather than one-off jobs.
truth: The $20,000/month example is a single real operator Zaback says he personally observed and spoke with, a specific and checkable-in-principle account rather than an anonymous claim, though it's still one data point rather than an industry average. The pet-waste-removal market size and growth figures cited ($537 million market by 2035) are framed as industry projections, not something Zaback personally verified.

name: AI avatars and virtual influencers
cost: Low startup cost, high time investment
what: Build a photorealistic AI-generated person using tools like Higsfield, then use that character to sell products or build a following as an AI influencer, earning through sponsorships and affiliate income.
pitch: AI avatars remove the usual friction of being an influencer, no filming yourself, no bad hair days. Tilbury demonstrates that the avatar generation itself takes only minutes.
best: Someone who's genuinely comfortable with a multi-month content and audience-building project, since the avatar is just the starting point.
truth: Building the avatar is fast, but Tilbury is upfront that developing a consistent character, engaging content, and an actual audience is a much longer process, likely months, not days. This is closer to a content-creator business than a quick service.

name: Fractional executive services
what: Offer part-time senior leadership, CFO, COO, or CMO, to businesses that need executive-level guidance but can't afford, or don't need, a full-time hire. You work with several clients at once, each paying a monthly retainer for a set number of hours or specific deliverables.
pitch: Package your judgment into a recurring monthly fee, typically $5,000 to $15,000 per client, and take on 4 to 6 clients at once, which can add up to real six-figure annual income without hiring a team or building a product.
best: Someone with a genuine, provable track record of running or operating a business, not someone who has only studied the theory of business strategy.
truth: Heacock backs this up with his own real hiring experience, he's personally used a fractional CFO in his own businesses, so he's speaking from the buyer's side too, not just the seller's side. That's a real credibility signal. That said, landing the first client still requires real, sometimes slow, relationship-based sales, this isn't a fast-start idea, even if the eventual payoff is strong.

name: The consume, apply, educate roadmap to a $10,000-a-month income
what: This is a general three-stage framework rather than one specific business, for building a high-income skill into a public, teachable business. Stage one is consuming targeted knowledge (picking one high-income skill like video editing, sales, or design, then learning it from credible creators and communities, not just random content). Stage two is applying it by taking on real, even low-paying, clients to build a track record. Stage three is educating others in that same skill once you've built real experience, through content, courses, or communities.
pitch: Tilbury argues the real money isn't in the skill itself but in eventually teaching it, since an education product (a course, membership, or community) only has to be built once and can be sold repeatedly for predictable, recurring revenue. He frames relatability, being visibly a few steps ahead of your audience rather than a distant expert, as the actual differentiator that gets people to buy from you over someone more credentialed.
best: Someone starting from genuinely little, no capital, no track record, who's willing to spend real time building a skill and a public presence before expecting income, rather than someone looking for a fast, passive result.
truth: The framework itself (build a skill, prove it on real clients, then teach it) is sound and echoes advice from other creators covered elsewhere in this database. Worth knowing: partway through, the video recommends a paid book-summary app and a course-hosting platform (Kajabi) as sponsored plugs, so those specific tool recommendations carry a financial incentive, separate from the underlying framework, which doesn't depend on either product.

name: Portable sanitation servicing (porta-potties and construction site rentals)
cost: Significant upfront equipment cost (units plus servicing truck)
what: Rent and service portable toilets and sanitation units for active construction sites, which are legally required to have them for the length of a build, as well as weddings, festivals, and outdoor events, charging a recurring monthly or per-visit fee to pump out, restock, and maintain each unit.
pitch: Construction contracts alone can run 6 to 18 months and combine a monthly per-unit rental fee with weekly service visits, and the same units can also be booked for single-weekend events, giving two very different customer bases for the same physical asset. The presenters argue this is one of the most recession-proof businesses on their list, since active construction and events don't stop needing sanitation just because almost nobody wants to be the one servicing it.
best: Someone willing to do genuinely unglamorous, hands-on labor (or manage a crew that does), and who has the capital to purchase the units as a real upfront equipment cost.
truth: The presenters are candid that this is deliberately ranked near the bottom of their list specifically because it's the least glamorous, most labor-intensive business on it, since you or your crew are doing the pump-outs and restocks yourselves. They frame it as a legitimate, demand-backed business rather than a passive one, and don't overstate how easy it is to get started.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Monetizing a curated Spotify playlist
what: Build a Spotify playlist in a specific genre or mood, grow its followers, and monetize it by giving independent artists a way to get their songs placed on it in exchange for payment.
pitch: There are two ways to charge for this: directly billing artists a flat fee per song placement, or running it as a Patreon-style membership where artists pay a small monthly fee for the chance to submit music for consideration. Tilbury prefers the second, since it's more passive (income arrives monthly without per-song negotiation) and feels more honest, since you're only picking songs you'd genuinely include rather than accepting anyone who pays. At $5 a month, 1,000 subscribed artists would be $5,000 a month.
best: Someone with a genuine ear for a specific music genre or mood who's willing to put in the upfront time to build a playlist's following before it has real placement value to artists.
truth: Tilbury is upfront that the direct pay-per-placement version violates Spotify's terms of service, and flags it as a real downside of that approach, not just a minor caveat, which is a good transparency signal. The Patreon-membership version he prefers doesn't have that problem. No specific real-world case study or dollar figures are given for either approach, so the $5,000-a-month math is illustrative math, not a demonstrated result.

name: Pressure washing business with a trash can cleaning upsell
what: Pressure wash residential driveways, patios, and building exteriors, then add a simple upsell while already on-site: offer to clean the customer's outdoor trash cans for an extra $20 to $30 per can, since the water, cleaning solution, and equipment are already there.
pitch: Zaback cites a personal acquaintance, a former financial advisor with no industry background, who started with a trailer, water tank, hose, and surface cleaner, and crossed $100,000 in his best single month four years in. He frames the U.S. pressure washing industry as a $1.2 billion market across 32,000-plus companies with consistent, non-seasonal demand, and notes average residential jobs run $400 to $1,000.
best: Someone willing to start with used or basic equipment and build a route, then compound revenue per stop by bundling in the trash-can upsell rather than driving to new jobs for incremental income.
truth: The $100,000-month example is a specific person Zaback knows personally, a real but individual result rather than a typical outcome, and it came after four years of operating, not immediately. The trash-can upsell math (an extra $40-60 per stop) is a straightforward, independently testable idea regardless of how the broader pressure-washing business performs.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Merch by Amazon print-on-demand t-shirts
what: List t-shirt (and other apparel) designs for sale directly on Amazon through its Merch by Amazon program. There's no inventory to buy upfront: you upload a design, pick colors and a price, and Amazon prints, ships, and handles customer service, paying you a royalty per sale.
pitch: Tilbury frames this against the traditional route of pre-printing shirts in bulk (multiple colors and sizes) and hoping they sell, which risks money on stock that doesn't move. Merch by Amazon removes that risk entirely since nothing is printed until it's actually purchased, and it also gives you access to Amazon's existing customer base instead of needing to build your own audience or attend events to sell in person.
best: Someone with design skills (or comfortable directing AI tools to generate designs) who wants to test apparel ideas without tying up money in inventory that might not sell.
truth: The illustration used, a friend who pre-printed thousands of shirts and could only capitalize on one design that took off, is a real anecdote but a single example, not a data set. Worth knowing separately: Amazon requires all designs to be either fully original or properly licensed, so using copyrighted characters or logos without permission isn't just against Merch by Amazon's rules, it's a real legal risk.

name: Compliance and risk-elimination services
what: You become the specialized expert businesses pay to eliminate regulatory risk, things like product compliance certification, HIPAA compliance, OSHA workplace safety, or R&D tax credit paperwork. Done well, this work can save a company millions in fines or lawsuits; done poorly, it can cost them just as much.
pitch: Heacock ranks this as his top category because it hits every trait that supports premium pricing at once: the work is recurring, it's genuinely painful for the business to do themselves, it's document-heavy, which plays well with AI-assisted tools, and, most importantly, the customer's name and reputation is on the line if it's done wrong. That combination means businesses will pay well above what the raw hours would suggest.
best: Someone with real experience who is willing to specialize deeply in one regulatory area rather than staying a generalist.
truth: In the video, Heacock uses a real anecdote to ground the pitch, he mentions paying $33,600 for this kind of service himself, which shows he's speaking from firsthand experience as a buyer. But when he ranks this category as the single best remote business opportunity, that ranking is his own opinion, not an audited industry statistic.

name: Building a vending machine route
cost: Low to moderate startup cost (used machines can be bought cheaply, or financed)
what: Place and maintain vending machines in local businesses (offices, warehouses, workshops), splitting a percentage of revenue with the location owner in exchange for the convenience of on-site food or drinks with no effort on their part.
pitch: Tilbury's illustrative example is a young operator who approached a workshop with an old, unprofitable coffee machine and offered to install three new machines at no cost to the business owner, handling all maintenance and restocking himself, in exchange for a 15% cut of revenue. That operator scaled to machines across the state, all generating passive income once installed. Used vending machines are widely available cheaply, and can be financed and paid off from the route's own profits.
best: Someone comfortable with the upfront legwork of finding good locations and negotiating placement deals, who's willing to handle restocking and maintenance (or eventually hire someone to) rather than someone looking for something entirely hands-off from day one.
truth: The industry-level figure cited (Selecta reporting over $1 billion in 2021 sales, up 3% year over year) is a real, checkable industry data point distinct from the personal anecdote about the young operator, which is presented as a story Tilbury witnessed rather than a verified case study with real numbers attached. The core advice, that success depends on finding the right locations and the right product mix for each one, is genuinely the hard part of this business, not a minor detail.

name: Building a vending machine route
what: Buy individual vending machines (new or refurbished) and place them in high-traffic locations like offices, gyms, factories, or waiting areas, then visit on a rotation to restock inventory and collect revenue.
pitch: The video cites a 2025 industry analysis putting monthly profit per well-placed machine at $200 to $500 after all costs, with location mattering more than anything else. It also cites a CNBC feature on an operator running a $300,000-a-year vending business on about 4 hours of work a week.
best: Someone comfortable driving a regular restocking route and negotiating placement agreements with property or business owners, without needing any specialized skill.
truth: As with the other entries from this video, the specific case study should be read as illustrative rather than a verified individual, but the underlying industry figures cited (profit ranges, the 95% five-year survival rate versus 20% for restaurants) come from named third-party sources (an industry analysis firm, CNBC) that can be checked independently of the narrative wrapper.

name: Small engine repair shop
what: Repair small engines, lawnmowers, generators, chainsaws, pressure washers, and line striping machines, for local landscaping crews, contractors, and homeowners, positioning yourself as the reliable shop with fast turnaround rather than a hobbyist who fixes engines occasionally.
pitch: The presenters argue this is a skilled trade that almost nobody under 50 is actively pursuing, even though every contractor with small engine equipment eventually needs it fixed and there's no national chain to call. The real opportunity, they say, isn't that nobody fixes engines, it's that almost nobody does it as a real, reliable business with an actual shop and same-day callbacks.
best: Someone younger who's willing to learn a genuine skilled trade and is comfortable with a business that gets noticeably slower in winter, since demand is seasonal for outdoor equipment.
truth: The presenters are upfront that this is one of the weaker "build a real business" plays on their list precisely because the labor takes real time to learn and the seasonality is a real constraint. It's framed as a good cash-flow trade, not an easy path to a scalable company.

name: The skill pyramid for turning an online service into $10,000 a month
what: A general framework, not a single business, for scaling any online service (video editing, copywriting, thumbnail design, social media management, and similar) into real income, built around four elements: positioning yourself to serve businesses rather than individuals, pricing based on the value/results you deliver rather than hours worked, building visible proof of your work so clients come to you, and using reliable systems (a CRM, clear deadlines) to stand out from competitors who miss deadlines.
pitch: Tilbury argues businesses pay fundamentally differently than individuals do: a $2,000 problem is trivial for a business already making $50,000 a month if it solves a real pain point, so repositioning the same skill toward business clients (e.g., editing for an entrepreneur selling a product instead of a small YouTuber) unlocks meaningfully higher rates without learning a new skill. He frames charging based on results (a Facebook ads specialist billing on revenue generated, not hours) as the single biggest lever for income, since it reframes the client's mental math from cost to profit.
best: Someone who already has, or is building, one specific online skill and wants a framework for pricing and positioning it profitably, rather than someone looking for a brand-new idea to start from scratch.
truth: The core framework (serve businesses, charge for outcomes, build visible proof, be reliable) is genuinely sound and echoes advice given independently by other creators in this database. The video also includes a sponsored plug for a CRM tool (Odoo) and an affiliate link for a trading platform partway through, both tied to a financial incentive separate from the core advice, and roughly the second half of the video shifts into general personal investing (savings accounts, index funds, individual stocks, crypto) rather than business advice, which is a separate topic from the roadmap itself.

name: Digital nail art printer service
what: A portable printer that prints a custom nail design (a photo, logo, or pattern) directly onto a client's fingernail in about 30 seconds, connected and controlled entirely from a phone, requiring no artistic skill or manicure experience.
pitch: A custom nail design at a salon typically runs $30-60, and this machine lets you offer a comparable service charging $15-40 per nail with only cents of ink and adhesive as cost, using a setup light enough (under half a kilo) to carry to a fair, birthday party, or quinceañera and set up a nail station anywhere with just a portable charger.
best: Someone looking for a very low-skill, event-based side income who's comfortable working in-person at parties, fairs, or pop-up events rather than a fixed location.
truth: The specific cost and price figures are consistent with what's publicly listed for this kind of device on Amazon and Alibaba, a reasonable, checkable range rather than an invented number. No specific named operator or case study backs the daily-client estimates given, so treat the income math as illustrative rather than a demonstrated result.

name: Trash can rollout and curb service
cost: Very low startup cost (no truck or special equipment needed)
what: A single-purpose subscription service: roll a homeowner's trash and recycling cans out to the curb on collection day, then bring them back afterward, with no equipment beyond the cans themselves and a reliable weekly schedule.
pitch: Zaback profiles a company called Can Monkey, whose founder got the idea watching a neighbor pull into his garage and leave the trash can sitting at the curb, then reasoned other homeowners felt the same way. That company reportedly has over 4,000 active subscriptions across 18 states with 500-plus runners, charging $49.99 a month per property, roughly $200,000 a month in recurring revenue, with a churn rate Zaback says is under 1%.
best: Someone looking for the lowest possible equipment barrier to entry, since the entire service requires no truck, tools, or inventory, just a route, a schedule, and consistency, well suited to elderly residents, second-home owners, and short-term rental turnovers as target customers.
truth: The company-level figures (4,000 subscriptions, sub-1% churn, $200K/month) are Zaback's account of a conversation with the founder during a business tour, a specific and named source rather than an anonymous claim, though not independently audited by Zaback himself. The core insight, that people will pay recurring fees for genuinely unglamorous, avoidable chores, is the same pattern that shows up across several ideas in this video.

name: AI workflow consultant for local businesses
cost: Very low startup cost (free AI tools)
what: Walk into a local business, a plumber, dental practice, or small agency, and ask three simple questions to find one repetitive task worth automating, then rebuild that task using free or low-cost tools like Claude and Zapier so it runs on its own, charging an upfront audit fee plus an ongoing monthly retainer to keep it running.
pitch: Hawksworth frames the pitch as a simple three-question framework anyone can use on a cold walk-in or call: what task do you do most and hate most, does it follow the same steps every time, and what does an hour of your time actually cost. He suggests charging roughly £1,000 for the initial audit and £300 to £500 a month to maintain the automation, arguing that businesses aren't really buying AI, they're buying relief from stress.
best: Someone comfortable approaching local business owners directly, in person or by phone, and translating a vague complaint about busywork into a specific, sellable automation.
truth: The pricing figures given (£1,000 audit, £300-500/month retainer) are the presenter's own suggested starting points, not verified case studies of what businesses have actually paid him. The three-question diagnostic framework itself is straightforward and genuinely reusable regardless of the specific price points.

name: AI-leveraged bookkeeping and payroll services
cost: Low startup cost, software subscriptions only
what: Document-heavy, recurring back-office services, bookkeeping, medical billing, or payroll, where AI now handles much of the document processing, letting one person serve more clients than before. No accounting license is required, just tool fluency and a chosen niche.
pitch: This work is recurring by nature, businesses need it every month, not once, and AI tools have lowered the manual workload significantly compared to a few years ago.
best: Someone comfortable learning bookkeeping or payroll software and who wants steady, recurring client relationships over flashier project work.
truth: This is a solid, learnable option, though it's more operational than strategic compared to something like fractional executive work. It requires real comfort with financial recordkeeping, not just general business sense.

name: Running a pest control or similar recurring home-service route
cost: Equipment and certification costs vary by state
what: Sign up homes onto a recurring monthly service plan (pest control, or similarly structured services like pool cleaning or lawn care), and service them on a repeating route rather than needing to resell each customer every month.
pitch: The video does the math on one hypothetical route: 82 homes paying $59 a month for basic pest control comes to $4,838 in gross monthly revenue from one technician and one truck, with the model scaling by adding additional routes.
best: Someone willing to get any required state licensing or certification and who's comfortable with physical, on-site route work and a truck.
truth: This is one of the more genuinely well-established, verifiable small-business categories in the video; recurring local pest and lawn services are a real, common small-business model independent of this particular narrative. State licensing requirements for pest control specifically vary and can be a real barrier or delay worth researching locally before assuming this is a fast start.

name: AI-powered lead generation for businesses
what: Use AI tools to find and qualify sales leads for businesses, then sell the qualified prospect list or contact information directly to companies who need new customers.
pitch: This is directly tied to revenue for the buyer, a business can immediately see whether the leads you're providing turn into sales, which makes it easier to justify paying for.
best: Someone with sales or marketing instincts who's comfortable proving results with real numbers rather than promises.
truth: Gadzhi rates this his top tier, calling it a real business need, not hype. Worth knowing: this is a mature, well-established category, meaning there's real competition already in the space, and some practitioners report that certain traditional lead-generation tactics have grown less effective as more operators have entered the market in recent years. A differentiated approach matters more here than in newer AI categories.

name: Fire extinguisher testing and inspection route
what: Inspect and tag fire extinguishers for offices, restaurants, warehouses, and apartment buildings on the legally required annual inspection schedule, building up a recurring route of accounts over time.
pitch: Every commercial building is legally required to get its extinguishers inspected on a set schedule, and fire marshals actually check for the tag, which means the law itself does the sales pitch for you. Once you're inspecting a building's extinguishers, switching to a new inspector means a customer has to re-explain their whole building to someone new, which the presenters say makes accounts unusually sticky once you land them.
best: Someone comfortable with slower, longer commercial sales cycles who's willing to build up a large route of low-ticket accounts over time rather than looking for one big score.
truth: The presenters are honest that this sits mid-list specifically because it isn't high-ticket per visit, so building meaningful income requires a genuinely large route and patience with commercial sales cycles. They note it's a fragmented market with no dominant national brand, a real and checkable structural fact about the industry.

name: eBay niche reselling with the account-warming strategy
what: Build an eBay reselling business focused on a specific under-served niche (collectibles, vintage items, refurbished tech, trading cards, gaming accessories) rather than competing broadly, starting by selling unused items from around your own home to build account history before investing in inventory.
pitch: Tilbury cites a specific creator, Kai Towers, who turned $400 into $317,000 within a year focused specifically on the gaming-accessories niche (replacement thumb sticks, retro memory cards). The pitch is that eBay isn't dying, real Q2 2025 revenue was up 6% year over year to $2.7 billion, but has pivoted from competing with Amazon on speed toward dominating niches where loyal buyers specifically prefer eBay. The account-warming tactic (selling household items first) is framed as a genuinely low-risk way to learn the platform's mechanics, build seller feedback, and generate starting capital before committing money to inventory.
best: Someone with a genuine interest in a specific collector or niche category, willing to build real product knowledge in it, since success here depends on knowing the niche well enough to source and price competitively, not just listing generic items.
truth: The eBay revenue figures ($2.7 billion in Q2 2025, up 6% year over year) are a real, checkable company-level statistic, a good sign. The Kai Towers case study ($400 to $317,000 in a year) is presented as a real individual's result but without account screenshots or independent verification, so it's a strong but unaudited claim. Worth knowing: this video is structured as a promotional funnel, each case study featured is a paid video series inside the presenter's own course platform, so there's a financial incentive to make each result sound as replicable as possible.

name: Custom tufted rug business
what: Use a tufting gun, a handheld tool that shoots yarn at high speed onto fabric stretched on a frame, to create custom rugs with a logo, character, or design, a process that would take weeks to weave by hand but takes hours with the tool.
pitch: A small rug costs around $20 in materials and sells for $60-250 depending on size and design, with a customer base spanning barbershops and streaming studios wanting branded entryway rugs to individuals wanting a rug with their pet's face or kid's name. The process itself is described as inherently viral content: posting a video of a rug being made tends to generate orders on its own without needing to actively find clients.
best: Someone who enjoys hands-on, visually satisfying craft work and is willing to post the process on video, since the content itself is described as doing much of the marketing.
truth: The cost and price figures are consistent with what's publicly listed for tufting kits and finished custom rugs elsewhere, a reasonable range. No specific named operator or verified sales figures are given, so the income potential is illustrative rather than demonstrated by a real case study.

name: Junk removal service
cost: Low startup cost (lower if you already own a truck)
what: Show up to a customer's home or property, quote the job on the spot based on volume, load unwanted furniture, appliances, or debris into a truck or trailer, and haul it away, getting paid in cash or card immediately rather than waiting on invoicing.
pitch: Zaback frames the U.S. waste collection services industry (projected to surpass $90 billion by 2030) as large enough that small local operators can carve out real income, citing $500 to $1,500 a day in realistic revenue for a single truck and $250 to $300 as a typical job price. He emphasizes that the real growth lever is relationships, real estate agents, property managers, and estate sale companies, since apartment turnover alone runs 40-50% annually and creates a steady pipeline of clearance jobs.
best: Someone who already owns or can access a truck or trailer and is comfortable building referral relationships with property managers, agents, and contractors rather than relying purely on one-off individual customers.
truth: The per-day and per-job revenue figures are Zaback's own stated ranges rather than a single verified case study, though they're specific and consistent with the kind of pricing publicly discussed across the junk-removal industry. The relationship-based growth strategy (property managers, agents, estate companies) is a concrete, actionable, and independently testable approach regardless of the exact revenue figures.

name: Private AI assistant built for a solo expert (consultant, solicitor, advisor)
what: Build a private AI assistant for a solo professional, a consultant, solicitor, or financial advisor, by loading their past proposals, FAQs, and other documents into a Claude Project, then instructing it to answer questions and draft new proposals only in that person's own voice and only from their own material.
pitch: Hawksworth demonstrates the entire build in a couple of minutes: start a Claude project, drag in roughly 20 past proposals and FAQs, and give it a single instruction to answer only from the documents provided and ask a clarifying question if the answer isn't there. He suggests charging around £1,500 to build it and £300 a month to maintain it as their workflow grows, framing the value as multiplying the expert's own existing knowledge rather than replacing them.
best: Someone comfortable working with solo professionals who already have a body of past work, proposals, FAQs, case files, to draw from, since the tool is only as good as the material it's trained on.
truth: The pricing (£1,500 build, £300/month) is the presenter's own suggested figure, not a documented sale. The underlying build process itself, a Claude Project scoped to a specific person's documents with a narrow instruction, is simple enough to verify and replicate directly.

name: ATM placement business
what: Buy and place ATM machines in local businesses like nail salons or convenience stores, earning a fee on every transaction, and scale by adding more machines over time.
pitch: A real example is cited of someone turning a $2,100 first machine into an $8 million a year company over time.
best: Someone based in the U.S. who's comfortable with local relationship-building and doesn't mind managing physical equipment across multiple sites.
truth: This relies on a single case study, which may not be typical, and it requires physically placing and maintaining machines in person, so it isn't a remote or location-independent business.

name: Small-scale residential property management
cost: Low startup cost (service-based, no property ownership required)
what: Act as the bridge between everyday landlords and tenants, collecting rent, arranging repairs, and handling move-ins and move-outs, for landlords who'd rather pay a fee than manage those tasks themselves.
pitch: The video's math: a solo property manager handling 50 doors at an average fee of $91 per door per month brings in $4,550 in gross monthly fees, with income scaling as more doors are added and a small team is brought on.
best: Someone organized and comfortable being the point of contact for both landlords and tenants, including handling occasionally stressful situations like repairs or move-out disputes.
truth: Per-door management fees and the basic mechanics described here are consistent with how property management is actually structured in the real world, a genuine, well-established service category. The 50-door starting point implies real existing relationships or marketing effort to land that many landlord clients, which the video doesn't address in depth.

name: AI automation agency
what: Build backend automation systems, beyond just phone calls, things like workflow automation, data syncing, or repetitive task elimination, that replace manual work for businesses.
pitch: This is pitched as the higher-ticket version of AI services: rather than one tool doing one job, you're diagnosing a business's operational pain points and building a broader system, which supports charging more per client.
best: Someone comfortable with more technical, hands-on implementation work than a simple one-tool service, and who enjoys diagnosing a business's specific bottlenecks.
truth: Gadzhi is candid that the real need is genuine and the upside is there, but execution and managing multiple moving systems for a client can get tricky in ways a simpler single-tool service doesn't.

name: Commercial dock and door equipment service
cost: Moderate to high startup cost (specialized tools, van)
what: Repair and maintain the dock levelers, roll-up doors, and dock seals that every warehouse and distribution center relies on to load and unload trucks, and sign accounts to quarterly preventive-maintenance contracts.
pitch: When a loading bay breaks, a warehouse can't load or unload trucks, so operators will pay premium rates for same-day emergency repair on top of standard preventive-maintenance contracts. The presenters point to the ongoing warehouse and e-commerce boom as a structural tailwind that keeps this market growing every year.
best: Someone with real electrical and hydraulic know-how, since this is effectively a skilled trade working with motors, sensors, and safety systems, not a business you can outsource entirely from day one.
truth: The presenters rank this in the middle of their list specifically because of the technical skill and safety risk involved, since it's your hands doing the diagnosing and fixing unless you eventually buy your way into an existing operation. They're clear this isn't a laptop business.

name: Brand deal flipping: a middleman agency between influencers and brands
what: Act as the connector between brands looking to advertise and content creators/influencers looking for sponsorship deals, negotiating and managing the partnership in exchange for a cut of the deal value, a middleman business similar in structure to how Airbnb, Uber, or DoorDash connect two sides of a market without owning the underlying asset themselves.
pitch: Tilbury cites Suhail Amin, who started this at 16 with no existing industry connections and now generates over $4 million a year working with major brands (Ubisoft, Netflix, Acer) and creators. The pitch leans on a real, cited data point: as of May 2025, Americans watch more streaming content than cable and broadcast TV combined, with YouTube the single largest share, meaning brand ad budgets are shifting toward creators faster than creators can independently negotiate for themselves, which is exactly the gap a competent middleman fills. A worked example: one brand booking 5 influencer deals a month at $7,000 average value and a 30% margin works out to roughly $10,000 a month in profit for the agency.
best: Someone comfortable with cold outreach and relationship management on both sides of a deal (younger creators and often-older brand marketing teams), since the core skill here is negotiation and trust-building, not content creation itself.
truth: The streaming-viewership statistic (Americans watching more streaming than cable/broadcast, YouTube as the top platform) is attributed to a real, named source (The New York Times, May 2025) and is independently checkable. The Suhail Amin case study, including the specific $30,000 profit in his first six months, is presented in detail but is a single individual's account, not an audited business record. The video is part of the same promotional series discussed above (each case study links to a paid course), worth knowing when weighing how polished the result sounds.

name: Desktop laser engraving business for personalized gifts
what: A desktop laser engraver that etches a name, phrase, or design onto everyday objects (tumblers, cutting boards, keychains, plaques) across more than 150 materials including wood, leather, acrylic, and painted metal, controlled from a phone and requiring no artistic skill.
pitch: A $5 tumbler engraved with a name can sell for $20, and an $8 cutting board with a phrase can sell as a gift for $35, since personalized items are described as rarely getting price-bargained by buyers. The customer base spans anniversary and corporate gifts to cafes and barbershops wanting branded signage, with predictable seasonal demand spikes around Christmas, Valentine's Day, and graduations.
best: Someone looking for a low-skill personalization business with wide material versatility and genuine gift-giving-season demand spikes.
truth: The cost and price figures are consistent with what's publicly available for this kind of engraver and its typical products, a reasonable range. No named operator or verified sales record is given, so the specific income math should be treated as illustrative rather than a demonstrated case study.

name: AI-generated English-practice YouTube channels
what: Use free AI tools to make simple videos of two AI-generated characters having an English-language conversation (with on-screen text), aimed at people learning English, then monetize through YouTube ad revenue and optional fan-funding features like memberships.
pitch: The entire production process is free: an AI chatbot writes the script, Google's free Flow tool generates the character images, and Microsoft's free Clip Champ generates AI voices and adds captions. Sarah cites one channel under four months old that gained 2.4 million views and over 90,000 subscribers in a single month, and confirms it's a monetized, revenue-generating channel because it has an active paid-membership feature (which YouTube only enables for monetized channels).
best: Someone comfortable being fully hands-off from the finished product's originality, since the format is intentionally simple and repeatable, and who's willing to treat this as a content-volume game rather than a single-video bet.
truth: The cited channel's actual monthly income isn't shown directly, it's estimated using YouTube's typical $3-7 per 1,000 views ad rate (RPM), which is a reasonable industry-standard estimate but not a confirmed number from the channel owner. The inference that the channel is monetized (based on it having membership features) is solid reasoning, clearly explained, rather than a guess presented as fact.

name: AI micro-tools built with Lovable, sold as $7-$20 digital products
what: Use ChatGPT to brainstorm small, specific AI tools ($7 to $20 price point) that solve one narrow problem for a niche audience, get ChatGPT to write the build prompt, then use the AI app builder Lovable to actually build the working tool and sell it as a digital product through a simple storefront like Stan Store.
pitch: Hamilton demonstrates the full pipeline live: she prompts ChatGPT with a specific client's situation (a daycare owner in Texas), gets a list of tool ideas (a daily child summary generator, an incident report assistant, a lesson planner generator), picks one, has ChatGPT write the exact build prompt, then pastes that into Lovable to generate the working tool in minutes. She sells finished tools like this through Stan Store with a low-price entry point ($17, discounted from $39) plus an order-bump upsell to a higher-priced companion tool.
best: Someone comfortable brainstorming and iterating with ChatGPT who wants a fully passive, low-price digital product rather than an ongoing client service.
truth: Hamilton discloses she has her own paid "operating system" prompt packs and a paid membership tier, and the specific prompts she uses in the demo aren't shown in full detail, only the process. The core mechanic, ChatGPT for ideation and prompt-writing, Lovable for the actual build, is genuinely replicable without her specific paid materials.

name: Solar panel cleaning service
cost: Very low startup cost ($500-$800 for equipment, no license required in most states)
what: Clean the dirt, dust, pollen, and bird droppings that build up on residential and commercial solar panels, restoring lost power output, using a soft-wash or low-pressure hose system, a squeegee, and a water-fed pole, typically sold as a one-to-two-times-a-year recurring package.
pitch: Zaback frames the sales pitch around reframing the service: it's not just panel cleaning, it's recovering lost energy output on an investment that may have cost the homeowner $20,000-$30,000, since regular cleaning can boost power production by 10-20% in dirty conditions. He cites the solar panel cleaning industry being valued at $1.22 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $2.57 billion by 2035, with especially strong opportunity in high-solar-adoption states like Arizona, Texas, California, and Florida.
best: Someone in a solar-dense region looking for one of the lowest equipment costs and least regulatory friction on this whole list, ideal for someone wanting a simple, low-overhead recurring-revenue service.
truth: The industry valuation and growth figures are cited as third-party market research rather than Zaback's own data, and no specific individual operator's income is given for this particular idea, unlike several others in the video, so there's no personal case study to weigh here. The core value proposition (dirty panels underperform, cleaning restores output) is a straightforward, physically verifiable claim independent of any specific revenue projection.

name: AI-personalized, trigger-based sales prospecting service
what: Feed Claude a prospect and a specific trigger event, a funding round, a new hire, a relevant post, and have it draft a short, non-pitchy outreach message that references the trigger directly, so a sales team spends less time hunting for leads and writing near-identical cold messages and more time on actual conversations.
pitch: Hawksworth's pitch is that this doesn't replace a sales team, it removes the boring research and first-draft-writing work that eats their week, while keeping the human conversation, which he argues is what actually closes deals, intact. He suggests charging around £1,500 to set the system up and £750 a month to keep it running and the CRM organized.
best: Someone selling into businesses that already have a sales team or process in place and just need the research and outreach-drafting work taken off their plate, rather than businesses with no sales process at all.
truth: The pricing figures (£1,500 setup, £750/month) are the presenter's own suggested starting points, not documented client outcomes. This kind of trigger-based, one-prospect-at-a-time personalization is a specific tactic within the broader AI-powered sales space that shows up across a lot of WAH creator content, and the underlying mechanic, feeding Claude a single prospect and trigger, is simple enough to test yourself before paying for training on it.

name: Equipment rental business
cost: Often $50,000 to $100,000 or more per piece of equipment
what: Buy commercial or industrial equipment, like compressors, and rent it out to businesses that need it temporarily rather than owning it themselves.
pitch: Presented as tax-efficient, since equipment can typically be fully depreciated, alongside steady rental income.
best: Someone with real capital to deploy and existing relationships or knowledge in a specific trade or industry.
truth: Grounded in the presenter's own real business experience with equipment needs, which lends some credibility. This requires meaningful capital and local delivery logistics, not a low-cost entry point.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Faceless video editing service
cost: None to low startup cost (free tools available)
what: Editing video content, short-form or long-form, for creators and businesses who post regularly but don't want to edit it themselves, working entirely behind the scenes through async communication like Loom and text.
pitch: The barrier to entry is low since free tools like DaVinci Resolve and CapCut cover most of the work, and a portfolio can be built using practice edits of existing public videos rather than requiring paying clients first. Presenter frames it as one of the fastest routes to first dollars: a typical 10-20 minute edit starts around $100, so 10 videos a month is $1,000 as a beginner, scaling with better clients.
best: Someone who wants fast, tangible income from a specific skill and is comfortable trading hours for dollars rather than building a scalable asset right away.
truth: The presenter is explicit that income stays tied to hours worked, so this doesn't become passive on its own. The $100-per-video, $1,000-per-month figures are presented as typical starting points, not guarantees, and rates vary significantly by niche and client.

name: Owning and placing private ATM machines
what: Buy an ATM machine, negotiate a placement agreement with a high-traffic small business (a gas station, barber shop, or small grocery store), load it with cash, and collect a per-transaction fee every time someone withdraws money.
pitch: The video estimates a typical machine handling around 300 transactions a month at $2.50 to $3.50 per withdrawal, working out to roughly $300 to $1,500 a month depending on location, for about 30 minutes of restocking and receipt-checking a week.
best: Someone looking for the most hands-off entry point on this list, willing to handle cash logistics and negotiate a placement deal with a business owner.
truth: Owning private ATMs is a real, established small-business model, not a novel or fringe idea, and the per-transaction fee structure described is accurate to how these machines actually work. What the video doesn't cover: cash-handling logistics and liability, and the placement negotiation itself likely requires more selling effort than the video's brief framing suggests.

name: AI chatbots for support and sales
what: Build support or sales chatbots for businesses to handle repetitive customer questions on their website or messaging channels.
pitch: A lower-complexity entry point into AI services compared to voice agents or full automation systems, since chatbot-building tools have become fairly plug-and-play.
best: Someone looking for the simplest, fastest entry point into selling AI tools to businesses, even if it means lower differentiation.
truth: Gadzhi is fairly blunt here: he considers this overhyped and easy to commoditize, meaning a lot of people offer a very similar product, which puts downward pressure on what you can charge.

name: Waste oil and grease collection and recycling route
what: Collect used motor oil and cooking grease from auto shops, restaurants, and small manufacturers on a recurring pickup schedule, a regulatory requirement for these businesses, then resell the collected oil to re-refiners for a second revenue stream on the same stop.
pitch: Businesses that generate used oil or grease can't legally dispose of it themselves, so pickup isn't optional, and once you're the hauler of record for an account, the presenters say customers rarely shop around since nobody wants to risk getting caught non-compliant. The double revenue stream, a pickup fee plus reselling the oil, is what the presenters say sets this apart from most other route-based businesses on their list.
best: Someone with access to real startup capital for a vacuum truck and the right hauling permits, and who's comfortable with revenue that partly fluctuates with commodity oil prices.
truth: The presenters flag this honestly as one of the heaviest startup-cost items on their list, requiring a specialized vehicle and permits before you can legally operate, and note the resale side of the revenue moves with oil prices rather than staying flat. They frame it as one of the least-known businesses on the list rather than a proven, widely replicated model.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Claude-generated Etsy digital worksheet bundles
what: Using Claude to generate downloadable PDF worksheet bundles around a specific problem or interest, refined for formatting in Canva, then sold as an instant digital download on Etsy.
pitch: The presenter shows real Etsy examples of worksheet bundles earning $200 to over $1,100 a month, some accumulating over $80,000 across several years, then demonstrates the process live: pasting a reusable prompt template into Claude, specifying only the topic and page count, letting Claude generate the full worksheet content, then spending about 30 minutes in Canva fixing formatting issues before exporting as a final PDF for the Etsy listing.
best: Someone comfortable doing a final polish pass in Canva rather than expecting a publish-ready product straight out of Claude, and willing to test multiple worksheet topics quickly to see what sells.
truth: The presenter is upfront that Claude's first draft needs real fixing, formatting issues, before it's sellable, a more honest framing than some AI-content pitches that imply zero manual work. The specific per-listing revenue figures shown come directly from each listing's own public Etsy sales-count display, a more verifiable source than some third-party estimation tools used elsewhere in this database. A sponsored VPN segment appears partway through, unrelated to the core worksheet-selling content.

name: Video editing for brand and influencer campaigns
what: Offer video editing services, starting with small jobs for individual creators and small businesses, then working up to editing paid brand and influencer campaign content, positioning the skill as a scalable freelance business rather than a one-off gig.
pitch: Tilbury cites Tom La Trousse, who taught himself editing from his university dorm room and built to $100,000 in yearly profit editing influencer collaborations for brands like Coca-Cola, Nintendo, and Gymshark. The pitch leans on video's dominance of internet traffic (cited at 82.5% of global internet traffic) as evidence of durable, growing demand, and directly addresses the AI-replacement question: the argument is that AI tools can automate mechanical cutting and beat-syncing, but can't judge emotional pacing or build genuinely original approaches the way a human editor does, so editing remains a real, in-demand skill even as AI tools mature around it.
best: Someone willing to start with smaller, lower-paying jobs (TikToks and Reels for small creators) to build a portfolio before pursuing higher-value brand work, rather than expecting to land major clients immediately.
truth: The 82.5%-of-internet-traffic figure is a commonly cited industry statistic, though its original source isn't named in the video, so it's worth treating as a general industry estimate rather than an audited number. The Tom La Trousse case study is specific (named brands, a dollar figure) but comes from the presenter's own paid course content, where Tom is a featured instructor, a real financial incentive behind how the result is framed. The advice to build a portfolio through smaller jobs before pursuing brand-level clients is sound, general freelancing guidance independent of any specific tool or course.

name: Resin 3D printed collectible figures
what: A resin 3D printer that hardens liquid resin layer by layer using ultraviolet light to produce highly detailed figures and objects, using thousands of freely available design files rather than requiring any design skill, and running largely unattended once started.
pitch: A single figure costs $1-3 in resin and sells for $15-50, with customers spanning anime and video game collectors, tabletop gamers needing miniatures, and even jewelers and architects wanting prototypes. The video notes the highest earners in this space typically sell bundles rather than single pieces, a set of 20 miniatures costing under $10 to produce but selling for $40-80.
best: Someone comfortable with a bit of a learning curve on printer setup and post-processing (cleaning and curing prints) who wants to sell into hobbyist and collector communities.
truth: The cost and price figures given are broadly consistent with what's publicly documented for resin printing, a reasonable range, though no named operator or verified sales figures back the specific claims, so the income math is illustrative rather than a demonstrated result.

name: AI-designed print-on-demand Etsy store
cost: Low startup cost (Etsy's $15 setup fee, plus enough cash or credit to cover printing costs until Etsy pays out)
what: Use free AI chatbots to brainstorm clothing designs and Google's free Flow tool to generate the actual artwork, then list the designs on print-on-demand apparel through Printify, sold via an Etsy storefront. Printify charges the manufacturing cost per sale; Etsy pays out the sale price minus its own fees once the item ships.
pitch: Sarah runs this business herself and is candid that it isn't entirely free to run, despite the AI tools themselves being free: Etsy has a one-time $15 setup fee, and because Etsy doesn't release the sale proceeds until after the item ships, you need to be able to front the manufacturing cost (roughly $9 on a $20 shirt in her example) before you're reimbursed. For anyone without even that small amount of float, she points to Printify's own free pop-up storefront tool as a genuinely $0 alternative to Etsy, which pays out as a royalty after Printify covers its own production cost.
best: Someone comfortable with basic AI image generation and willing to either front a small amount of production cash on Etsy, or accept a smaller, simpler storefront through Printify's free option instead.
truth: Sarah discloses she runs a successful version of this business herself, which is a real credibility signal, but also means she has a direct financial interest in recommending the specific paid tools she promotes alongside this content (a Canva Pro affiliate link and her own paid course). The core mechanics of the business (AI design plus print-on-demand fulfillment) don't require either of those paid products to work.

name: AI-written done-for-you content service for busy professionals
what: Use ChatGPT or Claude to write newsletters, blog posts, LinkedIn posts, and social captions on behalf of busy professionals, like doctors, plumbers, or founders, who know they should be publishing content but don't have the time, then hand them the finished, ready-to-post material.
pitch: Hamilton frames the pitch around convenience rather than the writing itself: professionals will pay for speed and ease, having someone hand them scripts and posts ready to use rather than having to write anything themselves. The pitch to a client is built around not making them do any of the work, not requesting information they'd need time to gather.
best: Someone comfortable picking a specific professional niche (rather than writing generically for anyone) and willing to do the outreach to land a first few clients.
truth: This is a fairly general pitch without a specific pricing example, client acquisition story, or verified case study in the video, more of a suggested direction than a tested playbook. The underlying mechanic, using AI to draft content a professional would otherwise pay a ghostwriter for, is straightforward enough to test cheaply before committing to it as a primary offer.

name: Window cleaning service for homes and businesses
cost: Very low startup cost (~$500 for basic equipment)
what: Clean windows for homes, storefronts, and office buildings, starting with a basic kit (squeegee, mop, bucket, ladder, cleaning solution) and quoting jobs by square footage and number of stories, with the option to sell recurring quarterly packages to homeowners and monthly contracts to commercial clients.
pitch: Zaback cites an average residential job of around $550, meaning six jobs in a day already crosses $3,000 in gross revenue, and profiles an Arizona operator who did $392,000 in a year with a small subcontractor team, starting with just $500 in equipment. He specifically highlights commercial accounts (restaurants, retail, offices) as more valuable than residential ones because they prioritize reliability over price shopping and will commit to standing monthly contracts.
best: Someone comfortable quoting jobs quickly over the phone once they know their pricing formula, and willing to pursue commercial accounts specifically for the more stable, less price-sensitive recurring revenue they offer over one-off residential jobs.
truth: The $392,000/year figure is a specific, named example (an Arizona operator using a subcontractor team) rather than an anonymous claim, though it represents one successful operator, not a typical or guaranteed outcome. The distinction Zaback draws between residential (price-sensitive, one-time) and commercial (reliability-focused, recurring) customers is a genuinely useful and independently testable segmentation for anyone starting this business.

name: AI content creation as a service using Claude and Higgsfield or Create UGC
what: Help e-commerce brands and local businesses create short-form product videos, ad variations, and UGC-style content without them ever hiring a creator, using Claude to plan the strategy and script (angles, scenes, voice-over) and an AI video tool, either Higgsfield connected to Claude for more custom control, or Create UGC for a faster, more streamlined workflow, to generate the actual footage.
pitch: The presenter frames the sales pitch specifically: don't say "I make AI videos," instead reach out with something like "I saw your product and had a few quick video ideas that could work well for your TikTok or ads, I can even make you a sample," which performs much better than a generic pitch. The offer is packaged into simple tiers, a basic package of one video, a standard package of three, and a premium package of five with captions and basic editing, sellable on Fiverr or through direct outreach to e-commerce brands and local businesses.
best: Someone comfortable learning a multi-step AI video pipeline (connecting tools, writing prompts, approving and regenerating scenes) who's willing to do a bit of manual editing to combine AI-generated clips into a polished final video.
truth: The presenter discloses this workflow depends on paid tools (Higgsfield and Create UGC both cost money per generation, and regenerating a scene you don't like costs double), and promotes a separate video and free cheat sheet for the full walkthrough. The core sales positioning advice, specific and personalized pitches over generic ones, is sound and doesn't depend on any particular tool.

name: AI content repurposing service for local businesses
cost: Zero to very low startup cost
what: Take one piece of long-form content a business already has, a podcast episode, webinar, or long video, and use AI to break it into a week or more of social media posts, so a business that made one good piece of content and then let it die gets ongoing distribution from it instead.
pitch: Hawksworth flags this as the idea he'd start with if he had zero clients and zero budget, since it needs no upfront tools or cash, just one business that's already creating content and wasting it. He cites one local business he did this for going from posting once every two weeks to multiple times a day, tripling their inbound inquiries in the process, and suggests using that first free or cheap result as the proof needed to land the next paying client.
best: Someone with genuinely no starting budget who wants a true zero-cost way to get a first result and testimonial, since the pitch here is explicitly to start by doing this for one business for little or nothing.
truth: The "tripled inbound inquiries" figure is a single case study from the presenter's own client work, not an independently verified result, though it's specific enough (once every two weeks to multiple times daily) to be a meaningfully checkable claim if you were working with that same business. The zero-budget, first-client-as-proof structure is a genuinely low-risk way to test the idea before committing any money.

name: Snail mail subscription club
what: A paid physical-letter subscription, around $10 a month, where a creator writes and mails personal letters, recipes, or art to subscribers each month, no email newsletter, actual physical mail.
pitch: One cited example grew to $60,000 in monthly recurring revenue within 7 months, built entirely through organic short-form video, with no pre-existing following required.
best: Someone with a genuine creative hook or personality who enjoys the tactile, personal-touch side of a subscription business.
truth: The numbers given are specific and credible, 2% churn, the first 1,500 customers coming from a single viral video, which is a good sign. Reliably mailing physical letters at scale, especially internationally, adds real cost and delivery-time considerations most digital subscriptions don't have.

name: HVAC or trade service business
cost: Low to start once trained, scales with team size
what: Learn a trade, HVAC specifically in this example, through trade school or working for an established operator, then start a capital-light local service business.
pitch: Framed as genuinely capital-light once you have the skill, since the barrier is training and licensing, not equipment or inventory.
best: Someone willing to invest real time learning a hands-on trade from the ground up before starting the business side.
truth: Grounded in the presenter's own real HVAC business, which is a credibility positive. This requires physical presence, hands-on trade training, and typically licensing, a genuine skill investment before any income starts.
